name: Strava
tagline: Log user-entered activities and map imported GPX files without recreating Strava's network

pricing.notes: Official US monthly subscription; regional pricing differs.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Unlimited-looking activity recording and sharing; 0 route creation/offline routes, 0 full leaderboards, and 0 advanced training analytics

tiers.name: Individual
tiers.limits: Routes, segment leaderboards, goals, advanced analytics, and subscriber features; 30-day trial

tiers.name: Family
tiers.limits: Up to 4 members in the same country
tiers.notes: $139.99 billed annually; price is unchanged if fewer than 4 people join.

tiers.name: Student
tiers.limits: Full individual subscription for an eligible verified student; 30-day trial

tiers.name: Strava + Runna bundle
tiers.limits: Annual access to both Strava subscription features and Runna
tiers.notes: $149.99 billed annually; annual-only and not eligible for standard discounts.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Free plan: no published activity-upload cap; 0 route creation/offline routes, 0 full leaderboards, and 0 advanced training analytics.
pricing.billingTerms: Individual monthly + annual; Family, Student, and Runna bundle annual only
pricing.hiddenCosts: Taxes can be added. Family remains $139.99 even with fewer than 4 people; the Runna bundle does not take Strava's teacher, military, medical, or student discounts.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Strava, log user-entered activities and map imported GPX files without recreating Strava's network. The hard boundary is athlete social graph, segment leaderboard, route data, device integrations, and scale, plus hardware data, content, coaching, and trust.
coreLoopDIY: Log user-entered activities, map imported GPX files, plan moderate routines, and show trends without recreating a social network or enforcing restrictive goals.
requirements: optional HealthKit or Health Connect permission
whatYouLose: athlete social graph, segment leaderboard, route data, device integrations, and scale
large content library and social network
moatNotes: hardware data, content, coaching, and trust
ongoingBurden: sensor permissions, data quality, notifications, safety language, accessibility, sync, privacy, content review, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Strava because people pay for polished mobile capture, trusted content, hardware integration, and coaching rather than the basic logbook. The recurring cost buys sensor permissions, data quality, notifications, safety language, accessibility, sync, privacy, content review, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: wger
priorArt.desc: Active open-source fitness and workout management application.

alternatives.name: Endurain
alternatives.desc: A private Strava-shaped box for GPX, TCX and FIT files; the social network stays deleted.

facts.install: Docker Compose with Endurain, PostgreSQL, and Redis; a bare-metal guide also exists
facts.dataFormat: Imported GPX, TCX, and FIT activity files plus user/server images live in the persistent backend data directory; accounts, activity records, gear, health data, and settings live in PostgreSQL, with Redis persistence for rate limiting and authentication security
facts.gapVsPaid: It imports and analyzes your activities but cannot recreate Strava's global social feed, segment leaderboards, route popularity, challenges and vast device/integration network.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker Compose, an environment file with secrets, host directories owned by the container UID, and a reverse proxy or TLS setup for safe remote use

alternatives.name: FitTrackee
alternatives.desc: Import activities, map them and keep the stats on your own server.

facts.install: Docker Compose with FitTrackee and PostgreSQL/PostGIS; PyPI, source, YunoHost, and NixOS installs are also documented
facts.dataFormat: Workout uploads, generated static-map cache, and logs live in host-mounted directories; accounts, workouts, routes, equipment, and other metadata live in PostgreSQL/PostGIS, with optional Redis storage for queued jobs
facts.gapVsPaid: It covers private activity maps and statistics, but has no Strava-scale social graph, competitive segments, heatmaps, clubs, challenges or integration ecosystem.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker or Python administration plus PostgreSQL 14+ with PostGIS 3.4+, secrets and writable volumes; multi-user email, exports, and archive jobs add Redis and SMTP

alternatives.name: RUNALYZE
alternatives.desc: Upload activities and get serious maps and charts for free; the social feed has been deliberately misplaced.

facts.install: Hosted account signup, then upload activity files or connect a supported fitness service
facts.dataFormat: Activities, health metrics, equipment, calculations, and account data live in RUNALYZE's hosted service; users can request a full archive and export basic datasets as CSV or individual activities in common fitness-file formats
facts.gapVsPaid: Its training analysis is deeper in places, but it deliberately lacks Strava's social feed, segment competition, clubs, route discovery and community motivation.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Subscription plan and a personal general-wellbeing tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Strava in an empty repository.
Use React Native with Expo, TypeScript, SQLite, and HealthKit or Health Connect only when explicitly enabled; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: log user-entered activities, map imported GPX files, plan moderate routines, and show trends without recreating a social network or enforcing restrictive goals.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create optional logs for activity, sleep, mood, energy, and personal notes with editable units.
Let the user build moderate routines and rest days without weight-loss targets, punishment, or competitive pressure.
Request health-platform permissions per data type and work fully without granting them.
Show weekly patterns and consistency with neutral language and no diagnostic or body-image judgments.
Add reminders that can be muted, data export, account-free local use, and full deletion.
Include a clear statement that the app is not medical care and should not replace qualified advice.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out medical diagnosis or treatment.
Deliberately leave out extreme exercise or restrictive-eating coaching.
Deliberately leave out wearable hardware, human coaching, and a large social network.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
